after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{10}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{10}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+1I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]+1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations which is already in row echelon form and has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=1.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+1I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]+1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations which is already in row echelon form and has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=1.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(5\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(5\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}-40 & 30 \\ 30 & 40\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

content.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
content.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(5\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(5\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}-40 & 30 \\ 30 & 40\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-24,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
after.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}(2\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{26}(2\cdot [\begin{aligned}25 & 5 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 25\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}26 & 130 \\ 130 & -598\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 5 & -23\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix
content.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-24,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
content.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}(2\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{26}(2\cdot [\begin{aligned}25 & 5 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 25\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}26 & 130 \\ 130 & -598\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 5 & -23\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
after.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}]+1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}]+1\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}]+1\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]+1\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
content.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
